questions.q: The Court's Marlborough line says labelling requires 100 per cent fruit from the region. Under which scheme does that 100 per cent rule actually apply?
questions.exp: In law, Marlborough is a registered GI held to the national 85 per cent rule for a stated region, variety or vintage. The 100 per cent belongs to Appellation Marlborough Wine, a growers' certification launched in 2018 that also asks for bottling in New Zealand and sustainably certified vineyards; it is a seal, not a legal tier.

questions.q: Into which climate category does the Court file both Gisborne and Wairarapa?
questions.exp: The Court lists Gisborne and Wairarapa as cool maritime, the class it gives Marlborough too, while Central Otago alone is cool continental. Both sit on the east coast of the North Island, sheltered from the westerlies; within that maritime frame Gisborne runs warmer and more humid, known for Chardonnay, and Martinborough in the Wairarapa is dry and windy, known for Pinot Noir.

questions.q: Which white grape does the Court's Certified list tie by name to Central Otago?
questions.exp: The Court's Certified whites for New Zealand are Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer and Riesling, with Riesling tied to Central Otago, where cold nights and a long dry autumn keep its lime and floral notes sharp; Waipara in North Canterbury is the other Riesling stronghold. Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay are the Court's Introductory whites.

questions.q: Of the five whites the Court lists for New Zealand, which two ripen to pink or greyish skins rather than green ones?
questions.exp: Pinot Gris is the grey-pink colour mutation of Pinot Noir, and Gewürztraminer the pink-berried aromatic form of Savagnin; given time on their skins either can show a faint copper tint in the glass. Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Riesling are green-skinned. In New Zealand Gewürztraminer made Gisborne's name in the 1970s, and Pinot Gris has spread quickly this century.

questions.q: Block 3 and Block 5, single-block Pinot Noirs from a biodynamic Bannockburn estate, come from which producer on the Court's list?
questions.exp: Felton Road, planted at Bannockburn in Central Otago in the early 1990s with a first vintage in 1997, is farmed biodynamically and bottles its Block 3 and Block 5 Pinot Noirs apart: the region's benchmark. Cloudy Bay is the Marlborough house of the 1985 Sauvignon Blanc, Villa Maria a national house founded in Auckland in 1961, and Ata Rangi Martinborough's great Pinot Noir name.

questions.q: Which social movement, named in the Court's history of New Zealand, kept wine off restaurant tables until 1960 and out of supermarkets until 1990?
questions.exp: The temperance movement held New Zealand drinking in check for decades: restaurants could not sell wine until 1960 and supermarkets until 1990, while Dalmatian settlers around Auckland kept winemaking alive on hybrids and fortified wine. The Court sets it beside the young industry, its innovation and the screwcap initiative of 2001.

questions.q: The Court asks a Certified candidate to know the Scott Henry trellis. How does that system train the vine's shoots?
opts: Upper shoots trained upward and lower shoots downward
Every shoot tucked upward into one narrow wall
All shoots left to hang from a single high wire
Shoots spread flat across an overhead pergola
questions.exp: Scott Henry is a divided canopy: the vine carries two fruiting zones, one above the other, with the upper shoots trained upward and the lower ones downward, spreading a vigorous vine's foliage to let light and air into the fruit. Vertical Shoot Position, the other system the Court names, tucks every shoot upward into a single narrow wall.

questions.q: Following the Court's pairing advice, which New Zealand wine would you pour with a dish finished with a fresh mango salsa?
questions.exp: The Court notes that New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc has the ripeness of fruit for sweet and savoury ingredients such as mango salsa, and that acid should meet acid: the wine's high acidity matches the lime and fruit of the salsa. Pinot Noir and Bordeaux blends are the Court's elegant non-European reds, kept for meatier dishes.

questions.q: By roughly how many months does a New Zealand vintage run ahead of the same year's Northern Hemisphere harvest, as the Court notes?
questions.exp: Grapes in New Zealand are picked from about February to April, while the Northern Hemisphere harvest runs from about August to October, so a New Zealand wine labelled with a given year was picked some six months before a European wine of the same year. A new Southern Hemisphere vintage can therefore reach a list first.

questions.q: Alongside Bordeaux blends, which New Zealand red does the Court offer as an elegant non-European option at the table?
questions.exp: The Court names Pinot Noir and Bordeaux blends as elegant non-European options: Pinot Noir from Central Otago, Martinborough or Marlborough for a guest who drinks Burgundy, and Merlot and Cabernet blends from the Gimblett Gravels of Hawke's Bay for a claret drinker. Pinot Noir is the most planted red in the country.

questions.q: Founded in Auckland in 1961, which house on the Court's New Zealand producer list grew into one of the country's largest wine companies?
questions.exp: Villa Maria was founded in Auckland in 1961 and grew into a national house drawing on Marlborough, Hawke's Bay and Gisborne, with reserve wines from single vineyards. The Court's three producers for New Zealand are Cloudy Bay, Felton Road and Villa Maria.
